To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

“Tumours arise by abnormal differentiation, and not by somatic mutation, and that the abnormal differentiation is due to the failure of cells to respond to the normal controls of differentiation, and that the failure is a result of the abnormal environment of the cells in their tissue of origin”.

(i) the cells in a tumour are not necessarily genetically identical; (ii) the cells in the tumour are not always clonal; (iii) tumour cells can be produced from normal cells by abnormal differentiation; (iv) abnormal differentiation can be induced experimentally by a wide variety of agents; (v) the cells in tumours can be induced to differentiate by a variety of agents.
the cells in a tumour arise as a result of abnormal differentiation, not mutation, and that they are not clones but mixtures.

the study of the nature and origin of the cells of tumours.
the question of the genesis of tumours.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
tumours are not clones of mutant cells, and that the process of neoplasma is not the expression of a somatic mutation.

neoplasms are the result of abnormal differentiation, and that they arise from cells which, in the normal course of their development, are destined to undergo a process of differentiation, and that this process is arrested or distorted by some factor or process which is extrinsic to the cell itself.
tumours are the consequence of a process of abnormal differentiation, and not of somatic mutation.

tumours are abnormal differentiations of the cell, not mutations.
